title: Saudi Arabia Postpones Its Flagship Investment Summit as Egypt Balances Houthi Attacks With a $5.3bn Saudi Deposit, and Japan Puts Coastal Missiles on Yonaguni
subhead: Riyadh cancelled the 2026 'Davos in the Desert' and told government staff to work from home under repeated Houthi strikes, while Cairo's parliament pushed its vote on sending troops to Saudi Arabia to October 26. In the East China Sea, US and Japanese forces began drills on Yonaguni, 110km from Taiwan, fielding the NMESIS coastal anti-ship system.

sections.heading: Riyadh Postpones FII as Houthi Strikes Reach the Capital's Everyday Life
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has postponed its Future Investment Initiative until next year, according to a statement on the conference website cited by Al Jazeera (AFP/Reuters). The tenth edition had been scheduled for October 26-29 in Riyadh. FII Institute chief executive Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud framed the decision as a commitment to deliver the 'full scale' the anniversary edition deserves; no new date was given beyond 'very soon'.

The move comes as the Houthis keep up strikes on the kingdom. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, quoted by TASS, claimed six operations in 48 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, against Saudi Aramco facilities at Yanbu and the Shaybah field, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Abha airport, the Khamis Mushait airbase and radar and naval sites. Al Jazeera reported that Saudi authorities say 13 people were killed in the October 10 airport attack and at least 18 across the airport strikes.

What distinguishes this week is the domestic effect. Government agencies in Riyadh told staff to work remotely Monday to Thursday, and companies in the King Abdullah Financial District — which houses major US firms — did the same, according to Al Jazeera's sources. The 99-storey Kingdom Centre, home to the IMF's regional office, asked workers to stay away. Speakers booked for the conference included Google president Ruth Porat, Goldman Sachs chief executive David Solomon and BlackRock chairman Laurence Fink.
sections.whyItMatters: The FII is the main annual showcase for Vision 2030 investment. Postponing it, plus remote-work orders in the capital, signals that Riyadh expects the threat to persist for weeks rather than days — and that foreign executives are now part of the risk calculation.

sections.heading: Egypt's Parliament Stalls the Vote on Sending Forces to Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
Egypt's House of Representatives adjourned its vote on authorising military support for Saudi Arabia to October 26, Al Jazeera reported (AFP/Reuters). A second session was postponed after the opposition Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its roughly dozen MPs to abstain, arguing parliament had not been told the mission's objectives, duration, cost or the risks to Egyptian troops. Members told AFP that most of the party nonetheless supports the measure.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take 'any measure' needed to protect its Gulf allies, while insisting: 'I'm not talking about confronting or attacking anyone. We're talking only about defence.' The National Defence Council approved the request on Sunday; under Egypt's constitution, sending troops on a combat mission abroad needs a two-thirds parliamentary majority. The Grand Imam of al-Azhar called on Arab and Muslim leaders on Sunday to mediate and avert further bloodshed.

The financial context is hard to separate from the security one. Al Jazeera notes Saudi Arabia is due to deposit $5.3bn into Egypt's central bank this month, plus $267.39m in interest. Egypt's foreign minister says the Suez Canal has lost about $11bn since the Houthis began attacking shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb in 2023. Turkiye and Pakistan have already made pledges under the Mecca defence pact signed in August.
sections.whyItMatters: Cairo is being asked to convert a financial lifeline into a military commitment. The delay shows the el-Sisi government wants procedural cover — and that the Houthi campaign is now pulling in Arab armies beyond the Yemeni battlefield.

sections.heading: US and Japan Put Missiles on Yonaguni as Drills Begin
sections.body:
The US and Japan began joint exercises on Monday that bring advanced missile systems to Yonaguni, the westernmost inhabited island of the Ryukyu chain about 110km from Taiwan, Nikkei Asia reported. The deployment includes the NMESIS ground-based anti-ship missile system, designed to deny enemy vessels access to a coastline — a mission set aimed at Chinese naval movement through the first island chain.

Yonaguni is a small island with a large strategic function: it sits at the northern end of the Bashi Channel, the waterway Chinese submarines and surface groups would use to move between the South China Sea and the Pacific. Putting a road-mobile anti-ship battery there narrows the sea room available to a Chinese force operating around Taiwan.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a permanent-feeling shift in force posture, not a headline exercise. A US anti-ship battery on Yonaguni shortens the distance between Taiwan and allied strike systems, and Beijing will read it as a direct change to the military balance around the island.

sections.heading: Kiev Says Washington Is Holding Up Missiles Europe Already Paid For
sections.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky told US senators on Monday that the Pentagon is delaying deliveries of air-defence missiles already funded by Ukraine's European allies, Deutsche Welle reported. According to DW, Zelensky said a Patriot shipment was waiting only for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature, and that allied transfers of their own interceptors were also pending US approval: 'The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine. But unfortunately, there is still no approval.'

The Kyiv Independent reported the same claim from a senior Ukrainian official and two military officials, one saying 'Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them.' Zelensky said the US delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors per month. The dispute sits inside a broader rupture: Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving sanctions mandated by the Lindsey Graham legislation and temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, writing on Truth Social that Zelenskyy 'doesn't want to end this war.' On October 19 he told reporters Russia 'has been fine on Ukraine,' per the Kyiv Independent. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington had paused intelligence sharing, while Kyiv says it again received no advance warning of inbound ballistic missiles; the night before, Russian strikes cut power to more than 500,000 households.

A separate report in the Kyiv Independent says Hegseth has also not approved the Patriot tranche under NATO's PURL mechanism. Washington has not confirmed any of the specific contract claims, and the Pentagon did not respond to the outlet's questions for attribution.
sections.whyItMatters: The argument is no longer about whether the US will fund Ukraine's air defence — Europe is paying — but whether Washington will let the weapons move. If a signature, not money, is the bottleneck, allied procurement becomes a lever the White House can pull at will, and Kyiv's winter air defence depends on US politics.

sections.heading: Sudan's Drone War Kills Over 160 in Days, and Ethiopia's Tigray Gets an Interim Authority
sections.body:
Medics and rights groups say drone attacks across Sudan have killed more than 160 people since Friday, Al Jazeera reported. A drone hit a transport hub in Al-Dibab, West Kordofan, on Sunday evening, killing about 80 people; 47 wounded were taken to Al-Mujlad, where 30 later died. A further attack on the RSF stronghold of Nyala killed 17, including seven RSF officers, while an RSF drone strike on displaced people in Blue Nile province killed 41. Both sides blame each other, and UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric said the UN is 'alarmed' by the strikes on civilians and central services. ACLED puts the war's death toll at at least 59,000; the UN says about 13 million people have been displaced.

In the Horn of Africa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has installed an interim administration in Tigray with six months to hold regional elections, DW reported. The move followed a September offensive by the TPLF and six allied armed groups that ultimately lost control of the region. Tensions with Eritrea remain unresolved — Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory, which Eritrea denies — and reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border persist, though DW notes the extent of any deployment is disputed.
sections.whyItMatters: Sudan's war is now being decided by cheap drones striking markets and displacement camps — a pattern with no front line to negotiate over, which makes mediation harder. In Ethiopia, a Tigray settlement that leaves the Eritrea question open keeps a second war risk alive in the same region.

sections.heading: Iran and Germany Trade Ambassadors, and the Houthis Hit Yemen's Army
sections.body:
Iran's foreign ministry summoned Germany's ambassador Axel Dittmann on Monday, Arab News reported, after Berlin summoned Iran's ambassador over an alleged plot to assassinate pro-Israel figures. A Hamburg court last week convicted a Danish national and an Afghan national of planning to target the president of Germany's main Jewish community group and the head of the German-Israeli society; the judge said the plot was 'orchestrated by Iran.' Tehran called the accusations 'baseless political allegations' and said it had no role. Separately, Al Jazeera reported that Tehran rejected any involvement in a plot to kill leaders of German Jewish groups.

On the Yemeni battlefield, Houthi ballistic missiles hit a military camp in Shabwa province, killing at least 53 recruits and wounding about 200, according to Yemeni military officials cited by AP. It was one of the deadliest strikes since fighting resumed this summer and shattered the 2022 ceasefire.

In the economic background, Brent crude closed above $110 a barrel on ICE on Monday for the first time since May 20, according to TASS market data, with December futures at $110.7 before easing to about $110.2. China's customs data showed Russian oil imports up 18.3% year on year over January-September, to 87.58m tonnes.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is now prosecuting Iran-linked plots in its own courts, which turns the Iran war into a European domestic security matter. And with Brent above $110, the Houthi campaign is being priced into global energy costs, not just Gulf security.

bottomLine: Riyadh's decision to postpone its flagship investment summit and move the capital's government offices to remote work shows the Houthi campaign has crossed from a military problem into an economic one. Egypt's delayed vote indicates Arab partners will move slowly and with conditions. Meanwhile, on Yonaguni the US and Japan are putting anti-ship missiles within 110km of Taiwan, and in Kyiv the constraint on air defence is now a Pentagon signature rather than a European budget. Watch two dates: Egypt's parliamentary vote on October 26 and Israel's election next week, where US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's unannounced visit on Monday, reported by Axios, points to Washington hedging on its own endorsement.
